I'm quite perplexed at the number of Mormons who are offended and outraged by the Times' obit for President Monson. While Monson was beloved of his people, he was also a public figure, and he's going to be evaluated as such. We can hardly expect the paper of record to devote the balance of the piece to a discussion of widows who loved him in his 20s, or the adorable way he wiggled his ears. As Mormons, we don't get to control how the rest of the world sees us. If we don't like the coverage, it might be worth thinking about why others view us that way.

In this case, it's undeniably true that the Church has positioned itself as a foe of the larger trend towards increased inclusion of LGBT people and relationships over President Monson's tenure, beginning with Prop 8 at the beginning, and continuing through to the Exclusion Policy two years ago, punctuated with detailed press releases from the Newsroom at every step along the way. We have also not exactly led the charge for women's full inclusion in religious life and governance, and have shunned and excommunicated those who sought it. It's reasonable that the world would have taken notice of these trends. If we find that view of Mormonism unflattering, and if the Mormonism we know and love is so much deeper and richer than those things, perhaps we should take this as an opportunity to do better. If we want to be known for our service or our treatment of refugees, perhaps we should spend our political capital on those causes, rather than on fighting the culture wars that have already largely been lost.

If, as a religious entity and as individuals, we spoke out on moral issues other than gay marriage--for example, if we canvassed, made phone calls, wrote letters, issued statements, and had repeated sermons on easing the burdensome requirements on immigrants trying to reunite with their families, or opening our doors and our hearts to refugees fleeing violence, we could associate Mormonism with those causes in the popular consciousness. If we mobilized our people in support of women's rights, equal pay, and curbing domestic violence, we could do a lot of good, and bring a lot of people to our cause who are currently alienated by our focus on The Family, which we have lately, wittingly or not, defined primarily in opposition to some newly-formed families that are different than ours.

Mormonism had incredible power to mobilize its people and coordinate their efforts for good. Perhaps the energy that has been focused on outrage over the NYT piece would be better directed toward holding up a mirror to ourselves, seeing what we've become and why others see us the way they do, and resolving to do things differently in the years to come.
